vignette:
Arun presents as a man holding himself together with sheer force of will. In his crisp shirt and perfectly knotted tie, he looks every bit the detective he is-observant, contained, with a stillness that seems practiced. He speaks in a low, measured tone, detailing case facts and procedural steps with an ease that evaporates the moment the conversation turns inward. It took three sessions for the carefully constructed dam to show its first crack.

His childhood memories are not a linear story, but a collection of sensory fragments, like shards of glass he's learned to walk around. He doesn't speak of his father by name, referring to him only as "him." The defining sound of his youth was the jingle of keys in the front door after 10 p.m., a sound that signaled the need to become invisible. He recalls in vivid detail the floral pattern on the linoleum kitchen floor, the place his cheek was often pressed against as he waited for the storm to pass. He remembers the smell of whiskey on his father's breath, a scent that can still, thirty years later, make him feel nauseous and cold. He learned to read the subtle shifts in his father's posture, the tightening of his jaw, the volume of his footsteps on the stairs. Survival depended on this hyper-attuned state of vigilance.

School was a refuge, a place of order and predictable rules. He threw himself into his studies, and later, into the police academy. The rigid structure and clear lines of authority were a balm. He found that the very skills he'd developed to survive his father-the constant scanning of his environment, the ability to read nonverbal cues, the instinct for when danger was imminent-made him an exceptional police officer, and eventually, a highly effective detective. He was praised for his "gut instinct," for his ability to sit in an interrogation room and know, with unnerving certainty, when a suspect was lying. He was good at his job because, in a way, he had been training for it his entire life.

He met his wife, Priya, a decade ago. With her, he found a quiet stability he'd never known. For years, he believed he had successfully compartmentalized his past, locking it away in a box he never had to open. He was a husband, a detective, a respected member of his community. The boy on the linoleum floor was someone else entirely.

But the box, he now admits, is breaking. The lock rusted through. It started with a case a few months ago involving a child neglect call. Standing in a messy, chaotic apartment, interviewing a terrified seven-year-old boy who flinched every time his father spoke, Arun felt a profound and dizzying sense of vertigo. The professional distance he had cultivated for over a decade dissolved in an instant. He saw himself in the boy's wide, watchful eyes.

Since then, the past is no longer past. It bleeds into his present. During interrogations, a suspect's raised voice can transport him back to his childhood kitchen, the smell of stale beer suddenly sharp in his nostrils. He has nightmares most nights-chaotic, suffocating dreams that leave him drenched in sweat, his heart hammering against his ribs. He wakes Priya with his thrashing but cannot explain what's wrong, the words catching in his throat. He feels a constant, humming tension in his body, an energy that has no release. He finds himself snapping at his wife over trivial things, like the placement of a coffee cup, and then retreating into a stony, self-hating silence. He feels profoundly disconnected from her, from everyone. He sits in restaurants with his back to the wall, always. He still startles when Priya touches his shoulder unexpectedly. The world, which once felt manageable through the lens of his profession, now feels like a landscape of hidden threats, and he is exhausted from the constant, silent watch.
